title: Solution Overview
subtitle: How PSTN2 makes every call verifiable, private and direct, without a central database.
endNote: Download the code and read the specification at pstn2.org.

segments.text: Many believe the answer to phone fraud is a central database, holding one national copy of every number.
But here is the breakthrough insight. All of that numbering information already exists, in each provider’s own databases.
We don’t need to centralise it.
We just need to ask the provider that holds it.
PSTN2 finds up-to-date information about a phone number directly from the provider that controls that number.
Each provider answers only for its own numbers, and any provider can ask any other.
That simple process removes the need for a physical central database.
PSTN2 enables real-time authentication to stop fraud, and direct routing to reduce costs.
End-to-end encryption protects privacy. And call branding means you know when it really is your bank calling.
Better emergency location data can enhance, or replace, today’s overnight updates.
And most importantly, an open messaging framework lets any process be automated, from porting to fault tracing and diagnostics.
Here is the key. Participation is optional.
Providers can adopt PSTN2 at their own pace, or not at all.
Calls between PSTN2 providers connect directly. Calls to providers that don’t take part simply fall back to today’s network.
No big bang. No forced migration. Just steady, voluntary improvement, driven by customer demand for new features.
Compare the two approaches. A central database is estimated at around £2m to build, and around £600k a year to run.
It would take years to deliver, and it would create a single point of failure.
PSTN2 has no central cost and no single point of failure. Providers invest no more than they would have done to use a central database.
Freely available, tested software cuts set-up costs, so providers gain value and make savings quickly.
And advances in artificial intelligence mean legacy systems can be integrated reliably without new APIs, a challenge once used as an argument against a central database.
Here is how a provider obtains all the available information about a phone number.
First, it checks its local cache, to see if it already has the answer.
Every PSTN2 response can carry an instruction to invalidate the cache, so cached values stay up to date.
If the cache has no entry, or the entry has been invalidated, the provider uses Ofcom’s S1 to S9 lists to find the Range Holder for the number block.
It then sends a request to that Range Holder.
The Range Holder may answer directly.
Or, if the number has been ported, it replies with a redirect, and the provider tries the new provider instead.
The provider updates its cache, and goes direct next time.
So there is no need for a central database.

scenes.title: One new field on Ofcom’s lists

segments.text: The root of all numbering information is each country’s regulator. This presentation focuses on the UK, and Ofcom.
The PSTN2 programme will also share how numbering data can be obtained in other countries, for global expansion.
For PSTN2 to work, the regulator adds one field to its numbering lists: the URL of the Range Holder for each number block.
Providers download and cache the lists, rather than querying them for every call. And other bodies can host copies, for resilience.
But the regulator may decline to host this field. Then another body would have to step in as the single source of truth.
That would create a new target for attack, and it would need strict governance.
So an early priority for PSTN2 is to persuade the regulator to host this one extra field on its numbering files.
Security is fundamental, and it is built in from the start.
Zero trust. Every message is challenged and verified, so a forged message is simply rejected.
Encrypt everything. TLS protects the signalling, and every call gets its own unique SRTP keys.
Data minimisation. Share only what is actually needed, and only with authorised parties.
Providers don’t need to build everything themselves. Some have no technical team, or only a limited budget.
Managed Access Providers, or MAPs, can host it for them: the PSTN2 API, number discovery, security and a web portal.
Small providers can take part without major investment. Larger ones can dip a toe in the water, to see whether the benefits are real.
MAPs compete on service and on price.
Existing wholesale carriers are expected to offer MAP services to their customers: a valuable new revenue stream, at almost no running cost.
Visit pstn2.org to download working code, read the complete specification, and join the move towards a safer, more secure telephone network.
